The biggest lie about the 2026 election is that the military won't be
involved.

In August, Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine assured Congress of the
military's "steadfast commitment to constitutional principles,"
[writing](https://www.slotkin.senate.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Caine_Response_8_28.pdf) that "the Joint Force has no
plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the
National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections."

Reassuring as that may sound, it is deeply misleading. For as Pete Hegseth
made clear last week, the military is undertaking an unprecedented role in the
election -- one that happens to violate the Constitution.

While there probably won't be the soldier boots-at-voting-booths nightmare
feared by some, the military is mobilizing a secret cyber force as well as
"every authorized asset, capability, and partnership" of its intelligence
apparatus to counter purported "threats" to the election, to quote Hegseth.

The administration is cultivating the idea that this is just the military
protecting against the most extreme cases like foreign governments hacking
into voting machines to alter results. However, military sources tell me that
the real focus is something far broader: the possibility of Americans'
political beliefs being shaped by foreign governments.

"Foreign malign influence" is the U.S. government's official euphemism for
censoring tweets, Facebook posts, TikTok videos and myriad other online speech
thought to imperil Americans' ability to think correctly. This is part of what
the military will be doing with growing intensity as election day nears.

As the national security system sees it, foreign powers like Russia, China and
Iran are busy eating through the foundations of American democracy like
termites, one social media post at a time. (Consider, for example, their
belief that American skepticism of AI data centers is the result of Chinese
influence, as [I reported](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/feds-think-ai-
critics-are-foreign) last month.) But the trouble with fumigating for termites
is that people live in the house. Since most Americans now live online,
foreign propaganda doesn't stay foreign: the moment an American likes or
shares a post, it also becomes an American's speech.

Yet Congress hasn't said anything about the obvious threat to Americans'
freedom of expression. And the hypocrisy at play here is mind-bending. Think
about it. Trump is still promoting his fanciful belief that the 2020 election
was stolen by foreign interference -- something half of Congress is happy to
condemn -- but when his administration directs the military to go after
foreign influence, none of them say a peep.

Both major parties, whatever their disagreements, share a consensus view that
Americans' beliefs and even voting decisions are not their own, but rather the
result of shadowy foreign influence campaigns. So much so, in fact, that
Congress has codified in
[law](https://www.law.cornell.edu/definitions/uscode.php?def_id=50-USC-690777767-2037611553&height=800&iframe=true&term_occur=999&term_src=title%3A50%3Achapter%3A44%3Asubchapter%3AI%3Asection%3A3059&width=840&utm_source=chatgpt.com)
a definition of "foreign malign influence" that of course focuses on "public
opinion within the United States."

Even if there's the best of intentions, the government using "public opinion"
and "malign" in the same sentence is dangerous.

The almost Greek tragedy level irony here is that involving the military in
elections is a greater threat to our democracy than all foreign influence
operations combined. Both the Constitution and federal law make plenty clear
that the military has no role here, and for good reason.

Not only are elections primarily a state and local responsibility under the
Constitution, but the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 prohibits the use of the
military to execute civilian law. An additional federal
[prohibition](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/592?utm_source=chatgpt.com),
literally titled "Troops at polls," traces its origins to the Civil War. In
1865, during Abraham Lincoln's presidency and in the final weeks of the war,
Congress made it a crime for federal officers to bring troops anywhere near
where votes were being cast. This was based on the common sense understanding
that the presence of armed soldiers is inherently intimidating to voters, or
at the very least is corrosive to democratic culture. But Lincoln couldn't
have imagined cyberspace, so the law forbids bayonets rather than military
botnets.

Oblivious to all this, Pete Hegseth announced in a recent memo that "the
Department of War (DoW) will effectively wield its capabilities to protect and
uphold the reliability of America's voting mechanisms against external
manipulation and disruption from foreign actors," before hinting at the
broader foreign influence focus.

To Hegseth, that means employing U.S. Cyber Command (CYBERCOM) and the
"Defense Intelligence Enterprise (DIE)" in order to "ensure that every lawful
voter can cast their ballot free from foreign intimidation, coercion, or
fear."

And what is the most hallowed civilian law of them all, one that the military
plays no role in "enforcing"? It is the inalienable right under the First
Amendment to the Constitution: Freedom of speech and the right of the people
peaceably to assemble. The military is not allowed to do anything to enforce
or otherwise intervene in that. And yet that's what Hegseth is doing here.

It might not be troops guarding voting booths. But the head of the Pentagon is
explicitly directing the military to guard voters in cyberspace -- it's not
that far off.

I'm alarmed how little attention is being paid to the military's unprecedented
involvement in our election. I really want to stay on this story and find out
what CYBERCOM is doing. Please help me by becoming a paid subscriber (or chip
